title: You looked at her… but you never saw her.
paragraphs: You looked at her… but you never saw her.

You saw a body.
A shape.
A fantasy.
A moment of selfish consumption wrapped in the illusion of admiration.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

Objectification is not just lust.
It is theft.

It steals personhood.
It strips dignity.
It turns an image-bearer of God into a product for private gratification.
And Heaven does not call that “normal.”
It calls it sin.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The modern world disciples men into consuming women.

Advertisements train the eyes.
Movies train the imagination.
Social media trains desire without covenant, intimacy without responsibility, pleasure without holiness.
And slowly, women stop being seen as souls.

They become categories.
Ratings.
Body parts.
Entertainment.
God saw it.
You knew.

The terrifying part is this: objectification does not begin in the hands.
It begins in the heart.
Jesus shattered the excuses when He said:

“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
— Matthew 5:27–28
The Greek language here is devastatingly precise.
The phrase “to lust after her” comes from the Greek:

ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
(epithymēsai autēn)

ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō) means:
to intensely desire, covet, long for selfish possession.

This is not merely noticing beauty.
Scripture never condemns recognizing beauty.
God Himself created beauty.
But Jesus exposes the internal corruption of possessive desire — looking at someone as something to consume rather than someone to honor.
Notice something else.

Jesus does not say the woman committed sin by being seen.
He places responsibility on the heart of the observer.
That destroys entire systems of blame-shifting.

The culture says:
“She tempted me.”

Jesus says:
“No. Your heart revealed you.”
Read that again.
In Scripture, women are never presented as objects for male consumption.
They are image-bearers.
Genesis 1:27 says:
“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.”
The Hebrew phrase for “image of God” is:

בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים
(b’tselem Elohim)
“Tselem” means image, likeness, representation.

Women are not lesser reflections of God’s creative dignity.
They are fully human, fully bearing divine image.
To objectify a woman is to dishonor someone stamped with God’s likeness.
And this sin becomes darker when we realize how Scripture describes purity of vision.
Jesus said:

“The lamp of the body is the eye.”
— Matthew 6:22

The Greek word for eye:
ὀφθαλμός (ophthalmos)
In Jewish understanding, the eye represented not merely vision but moral perception and inner condition.
Your eyes reveal your worship.
What you repeatedly consume shapes your soul.
Pornography, lust culture, voyeurism, obsessive fantasy — these are not harmless habits.
They are spiritual formation.
Every repeated act of objectification trains the heart to love selfish pleasure more than sacrificial covenant.
That is why pornography is so spiritually destructive.

It teaches people to separate bodies from souls.
Pleasure from responsibility.
Sex from covenant.
Desire from love.
And eventually, real people become disappointing because fantasy trained the mind to consume rather than cherish.
The enemy wants men addicted to images because addicted men rarely become holy men.
And women suffer under this system too.

Many begin to internalize objectification.
They feel pressured to market themselves for validation.
To equate worth with attention.
To compete for visibility in a culture addicted to exposure.
But Scripture never defines a woman’s value by lustful attention.
In Proverbs 31:30:
“Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.”
The Hebrew word for “vain” is:

הֶבֶל
(hevel)
It means vapor, breath, temporary mist.

External beauty fades.
Godly character endures into eternity.

This does not mean beauty is evil.
It means beauty was never designed to be worshipped.
Only God deserves worship.
Paul speaks directly to the issue of purity and honor in 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5:
“For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication.”
The Greek word for sanctification is:

ἁγιασμός
(hagiasmos)

Meaning:
set apart unto holiness.

Sexual purity is not repression.
It is restoration.

God is not trying to destroy desire.
He is trying to redeem it.

Because holy desire protects.
Selfish desire consumes.
There is a massive difference.

Biblical love says:
“How do I honor you before God?”

Lust says:
“How do I use you for myself?”

One sacrifices.
The other devours.
This is why Paul commands in Philippians 4:8:
“Whatsoever things are pure… think on these things.”
The Greek word for pure:

ἁγνός
(hagnos)

Meaning:
clean, morally unstained, sacred.

Purity is not merely external behavior.
It is internal alignment with God’s holiness.
And some reading this know exactly what conviction feels like right now.
Because this was never just “a little issue.”

You built secret worlds in your mind.
You normalized degrading humor.
You consumed women digitally while pretending to respect them publicly.
God saw it.
You knew.
But here is where the Gospel enters the story.

Jesus Christ did not come merely to condemn lustful hearts.
He came to cleanse them.
The same Savior who confronted sexual sin also restored broken sinners.
To the woman caught in adultery, He said:

“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
— John 8:11
Notice both grace and truth.

Not condemnation without hope.
Not acceptance without repentance.
Grace that transforms.
The cross exposes how serious sin really is.

Jesus did not die because lust was “no big deal.”
He died because sin destroys souls, relationships, marriages, identity, and worship itself.
But through repentance and faith, the heart can be remade.
The Greek word for repentance is:

μετάνοια
(metanoia)

Meaning:
a change of mind that results in a transformed life.

True repentance is not guilt alone.
It is surrender.

It is saying:
“Lord, my eyes belong to You now.”
And the Holy Spirit can retrain what sin distorted.

Men can learn to see women as sisters in Christ rather than objects.
Women can learn their worth is rooted in God, not public validation.
Purity can become possible again.
Not through human willpower alone, but through the transforming power of Christ.
This generation desperately needs holy vision.

Because when women are objectified:
marriages decay,
families fracture,
trafficking increases,
abuse spreads,
souls grow numb.

Objectification is not “small.”
It is civilization-level corruption flowing from hearts disconnected from God.
And yet Jesus still saves people trapped in it.
That is the hope.

Not self-improvement.
Not behavior modification.
Transformation through Christ.
If conviction hit you while reading this, do not suppress it.
That discomfort may be mercy.

Confess the sin.
Bring hidden habits into the light.
Cut off what feeds lust.
Stop protecting what Christ died to free you from.
And if you follow Jesus publicly while feeding secret impurity privately, understand this clearly:
God is not fooled by curated holiness.
He looks at the heart.
Maybe that sentence pierced deeper than you expected.
Good.
Because healing begins where honesty starts.
There is more waiting than shallow religion.
